newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bulldozers begin Jerusalem settlement. [CORRECTED 23:47 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bulldozers begin Jerusalem settlement. [CORRECTED 23:47 GMT]

text.p: Israeli bulldozers under heavy guard ploughed up a hillside for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on Tuesday (corrects from Thursday), opening a new chapter in the bloody battle for control of the holy city.

Israeli forces prepared for a Palestinian backlash after the groundbreaking that has pitted Israel's right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and drawn criticism from the United States, Britain, France, the United Nations and the Arab world.

About 50 Palestinian youths hurled stones from Um Tuba village at the edge of the site, a pine-covered hill known as Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa in Hebrew, between Jerusalem and Bethlehem. They burned tyres and blocked a road.

Police kept back and no injuries were reported. It was a foretaste of the unrest that both Israeli and Palestinian security sources fear will break out. A handful of youths also scuffled with troops at another nearby site.
"It is a black day for the peace process," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters.
Erekat later met Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh but neither side gave details of their talks.

Arafat called an emergency meeting to discuss the project, which tightens Israel's grip on Jerusalem and stregthens its hand at negotiations on the final status of the city that were supposed to resume this week.
Netanyahu denied that the housing for 6,500 Jews would torpedo U.S.-sponsored peacemaking.
"I am sure that the peace process will continue," Netanyahu told a news conference for the foreign media.
He said predictions of doom were "hyperbole".

But French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette called Israel's construction of the settlement "an obstacle to peace" and warned against a resurgence of violence in the region, echoing comments by Britain and the U.N. Secretary-General.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright urged a return to negotiations, voicing hopes there would be no violent Palestinian reaction.
But Faisal al-Husseini, the senior PLO official in Jerusalem, said at a protest tent-camp opposite the bulldozers that Palestinians' only option now was "to go down to the streets".
"I believe there will be an explosion if we don't solve this problem," Husseini said.
In Amman, the Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas, which opposes the 1993 peace deal between the PLO and Israel, called for a Palestinian uprising to protest the start of work.
"The Palestinian Authority should answer the call of the Palestinian people to go into continuous intifada (uprising)," Hamas spokesman Ibrahim Ghoshe told Reuters.
In Gaza, Arafat told reporters he had urged his people not to resort to violence. "I have done it," he said, when asked if he had issued the appeal.

Israeli security sources said troops were ready prevent a repetition of the violence of last September when the newly-elected Netanyahu opened a tunnel entrance near Moslem and Jewish holy places in Jerusalem. For the first time, Palestinian police used their guns to protect protesters. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israelis died in three days of gunbattles.
The Israeli army said it barred Israelis from entering PLO-ruled areas on Tuesday and suspended joint patrols with PLO police "because of the existing tensions".
The Palestinian Health Ministry declared a state of emergency at hospitals in self-ruled parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, an official at Ramallah hospital said.
Officials from both sides said chances of an Arafat-Netanyahu meeting seemed slim.
Arafat wants building stopped before a summit. He spurned Netanyahu's appeals to meet him late on Monday, drawing Israeli accusations the Palestinian leader was trying to stoke already high tensions.

Netanyahu seemed to be manoueuvering to lay any blame for violence on Arafat. He said the Palestinian Authority had recently released jailed members of Hamas, the group responsible for suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel last year.

"I am saying that our intelligence shows very clearly, unmistakably, that the Palestininan leadership has given the green light to the worst terrorist organisations in the world to go ahead with the kind of bus bombings and suicide attacks -- the kind of mass killings that brought a halt to the peace process," he said.
Palestinian security sources dismissed the charge as baseless.
Netanyahu forged ahead with the settlement under pressure from the Jewish settler and nationalist right of his coaltion.
The housing will complete a ring of concrete around the half of Jerusalem that Israel occupied along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1967.

Only a handful of protesters slipped through police and army lines to sit in front of the four bulldozers that began ploughing an access road. Most were left-wing Israeli and Palestinian-Israeli members of parliament.
